utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. It still registered. Okay. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, appearances in order of seniority: Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin, along with my co-counsel Milka Maglov and my legal assistant Tania Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, and I represent General Talic. Before beginning, I should like to inform the Chamber that yesterday we filed a motion -- or rather, a response to the Prosecution motion regarding two witnesses for the admission of their statements under 92 bis. Unfortunately, two errors crept into that motion, and I wish to convey my excuses to Your Honours and also to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecution, and to inform you that we filed corrections today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I have it in my Chamber -- I was waiting for the translation. I just went through it in French, but I don't have the corrected versions, or the corrections. So I will wait for those. Good afternoon to you. Preliminaries? Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman remarked as he walked in that something must be seriously wrong if there were three of us here today. It's not actually the case. Your Honour, I'm here really to tender my apologies on behalf of myself and Mr. Cayley that neither of us can be here this afternoon. As Your Honour knows, Stakic started this morning, and I have to deal -- or I have to see the witness for tomorrow this afternoon, and I have to get back to Stakic tomorrow morning. That's what you might call all-go at the moment. So that's the real reason I'm here; to apologise. But while I am here, can I just deal with a couple of matters that I understand that Your Honour raised. First of all -- or rather, Mr. Ackerman raised yesterday. One was the question of the sitting hours and translation. Your Honour, we discussed the matter, and it seems to us that it really must be subject to Your Honours' rulings, obviously, matter for the interpreters, if they feel that they can't cope with short breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. But the information I received during the break did not exactly tally with what Mr. Ackerman had said. I mean, it's something which is going to be verified, of course. And as I said, the last thing that this Chamber would try to do is to inconvenience the interpreters. I know how difficult their job is and how demanding it is on the mental powers of concentration. So you can rest assured that we will take everything into consideration and we will make any adjustments that may become necessary as we go along. I am informed, however, that the problem was not exactly what Mr. Ackerman mentioned or how he described it. In any case, it's being checked by Madam Registrar, and I'm being kept informed. As for today, I think we are going to maintain -- maintain the same schedule as yesterday except that there will be times when we will break for five minutes only, giving the technicians time -- enough time to change the tapes, which I understand have to be changed every hour and 40 or 45 minutes, instead of every two hours. So -- but that is being taken care of. I do appreciate your concern for the interpreters, Ms. Korner. I think we all share the same concern. We know how precious they are and how useful and dedicated they are to the work of this Trial Chamber -- to this Tribunal, not just this Trial Chamber. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then two other matters. First, in respect of the time that will be required to deal with the application on behalf of the journalist to set aside the witness summons on the 10th of May, Your Honour, I would say that the maximum two hours, and probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But would that include Mr. Robinson's intervention, the lawyer, in other words, your -- possibly your intervention, and any anticipated interventions from the Defence teams, or just -- or just Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's -- really, we're working on the basis that it -- Mr. Robertson is going to apply to set aside the witness summons, grounds at the moment unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And we would respond. But obviously, I suppose -- well, no. Your Honour, I don't think unless Your Honours were to allow either Defence team to intervene, it's not really a matter for the Defence. We have issued -- no, I'm sorry, Your Honours have issued a witness summons, a lawful witness summons. Mr. Robertson is going to object, we're going to respond, and I think it's a matter, Your Honour, whether the Defence have a right to intervene. I see Mr. Ackerman straight up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that point is taken. There is another point -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally agree with Ms. Korner, as we would say in Texas, I don't have a dog in that fight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that perhaps after having heard Mr. Robertson's submissions, we decide to give an oral judgement decision, say, the same day, are you anticipating that the journalist would be present here in The Hague or to give evidence immediately, or do you plan having him here at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- the idea would be that he's here. And then if Your Honour rules that the witness summons should not be set aside, he'd give evidence. I understand that he won't be here. I rather feel that if the ruling goes against Mr. Robertson, there may be an appeal. But as I understand the matter -- and I'm reluctant really to go into detail -- he won't be here. But I will make -- I will make further inquiries. As Your Honour knows, I have to reply to the request that was made by the solicitors in respect of the transcripts, which Your Honours have now ruled may be given. And I will ask whether the journalist intends to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you can fit in Mr. Robertson -- not Mr. Robertson, his client, the journalist -- anywhere within your witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would be preferable, Your Honour, obviously to deal with him straight away, because it's close to the Banja Luka evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. And this is why I'm asking actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think Your Honour -- I'm going to make some further inquiries as to whether he would be here. Because if he is, then we can deal with -- it's very short evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. This is why I consider -- I mean, there may be a principle involved. Mr. Robertson may be -- but it's not that important, because there was a decision by the Supreme Court of the United States precisely these last days. But somewhat -- somewhat different. And it was disposed of because the matter such became moot in the meantime. So -- but anyway, let's leave it at that, and then we'll take it up on the 10th of May. In the meantime, I told Mr. Cayley and Mr. Koumjian and I think Ms. Sutherland as well, that we will make any adjustments as they may become necessary as we approach the date. But with the understanding that Mr. Robertson's submissions will take place during a normal session. In other words, not going to invent another extra session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, that in fact -- that really leads into the final matter that I wish to raise this afternoon, because it would fit in very nicely in a sense because that week where we don't sit until the Tuesday has been set aside for the first of the witnesses from the humanitarian organisation. Now, Your Honour, that leads me on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman has put in a motion saying that he wants it -- that evidence delayed because of -- he's not received any assistance so far. And in addition to that, the translation of Madam Fauveau's rule -- submission on the Rule 70 aspect has also been received. Your Honour, we can deal with Mr. Ackerman's submissions very quickly, verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I was getting to. As soon as you finish --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And it may be -- I haven't had a chance to read through the translation, although, like Your Honour, I read the French but I'm always a bit nervous as to whether I've got the right meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. We are exactly in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, I'd want to consider it. But it may be that we feel at the end of the day that the submissions made by Madam Fauveau are pretty much the same as those made by Mr. Ackerman, to which we've already responded. And so we don't want to respond further. What I was going to suggest was that tomorrow, after the witnesses that Ms. Sutherland is calling have completed and before I call the next witness, if we feel we've already dealt with Madam Fauveau's motion, I could deal orally with Mr. Ackerman's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would be the fastest way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That would be extremely useful, in particular for two reasons -- main reasons: One is that we have been working and we are already, I would say, in a -- at an advanced stage in our research on the submissions made on Mr. Ackerman's motion on 70, particularly one part of Rule 70. In the meantime, of course, the response of General Talic, of Madam Fauveau, has come in, which I looked into again this morning. I do not anticipate our decision to be delayed much on -- on this matter. I would also anticipate that this is something which is fundamentally important -- an issue which is fundamentally important, and whichever way it goes, I would anticipate that there be an appeal. It is also a matter which does not necessarily imply -- say, if it is decided in favour of Mr. Ackerman in whole or in part, I would like you to consider the possibility, if not the probability, that it does not necessarily entail that the witnesses from the particular humanitarian organisation cannot be produced. What is involved is something completely different and which will be decided in favour or against but which may not exactly have a bearing on whether your intended witnesses ought to be produced or not. So that is something which, if you're going to discuss it tomorrow, I would like you to take into -- take into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid at this stage, Your Honour, having aroused my interest somewhat, I'm somewhat at a loss to know -- I can't -- until Your Honours have issued a ruling --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- I can't deal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, no. Because there is a possibility that part of Rule 70 may not exactly comply with the basic principles. Let's say that, for argument's sake, we decide that. But that opens the door -- one or more doors for the Defence. It doesn't necessarily close the doors which you already have opened to produce witnesses from that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this is gripping, Your Honour. So I think I'll have to wait for the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I want you -- this is what I want you to think about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as best we can, we'll think about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And we will discuss it tomorrow. Tomorrow, do you anticipate to be present at the beginning or towards the end of the session?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall be present at the beginning depending on -- although I know, as usual, the short administrative matters have taken a little long, I am anticipating, I hope, that even if there is a little bit left over of the witness coming next, we will be starting with another witness. So I will be here from 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if Your Honour -- unless there is any other matter I can assist on, if Your Honour will excuse me from the rest of the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly I will. Okay. So anything else? Can we call the witness now, please. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Fazlagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be your last day before this Chamber. And I kindly ask you to make the same solemn declaration that you made yesterday and last Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Fauveau-Ivanovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the last train leaving Banja Luka and you said that the last train for Croatia left towards the end of 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that trains were no longer leaving for Croatia after that date because of the combat operations going on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the last train for Sarajevo left at the end of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any trains for Belgrade after that date?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there buses for Belgrade after that period?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout, all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In May, June 1992, there were buses for Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but when the corridor was broken through, then traffic was established with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. But before the corridor operation took place, were there any buses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a period when Banja Luka was entirely cut off from the world.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When JAT established airlines with Belgrade, were the buses still going to Belgrade? And please give me an answer only if you know it.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, sir, that you remember that only Muslims and Croats were leaving Banja Luka in April and May 1992. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Persons who were buying tickets, did you personally have any contact with them, or did those people go to buy their tickets at the ticket counter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the counter, with the exception of a few cases -- of some cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the regular passengers were buying tickets at the counter. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were not at the counter, were you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the people who were buying tickets were only Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in 100 per cent of the cases. There probably was a certain number but a symbolic number of people of Serb ethnicity. But I know because I frequently went to the airport and I saw there mostly -- mostly in 90 something per cent of the cases -- that they were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people that you saw, did you know them? The people that you saw at the airport, did you know them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you allowed for the possibility that some of the tickets were resold afterwards for a higher price. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only assume that, because I heard that this was happening at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, it was Muslims and Croats who were selling tickets to other Muslims and Croats for a higher price.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. It's more probable that it was the other way around, because many people who couldn't get a ticket went directly to the airport to try and board a plane in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you're not sure and that it was more probable that it was the other way around, what did you mean? I didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps somebody took advantage of the situation then and perhaps managed to get a hold of two or three tickets more than they needed, so they engaged in a business transaction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: In those cases, was it non-Serbs reselling tickets to other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was only non-Serbs who were buying tickets in your agency, how could Serbs be reselling those tickets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not -- the possibility cannot be excluded that some Serbs didn't buy tickets. I didn't claim that this happened in 100 per cent of the cases, that they were all non-Serbs. For instance, there was other -- there were other agencies like INEX, the INEX agency, which was privately owned by a Serb. And then there was another privately owned agency by a young woman, of Serb ethnicity again, who came to our agency because they were not allowed to sell tickets directly, so they would come to our agency and buy a certain number of tickets. I assume for friends of theirs or for some other purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about another agency, the Putnik agency.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that their main activity was the sale of plane tickets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Especially in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that you believed that the last flight from Banja Luka to Belgrade left around the 18th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 18th of May, what were the activities of the Putnik agency? What was it doing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Virtually nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that agency closed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Hamdija Trnovac its director until it closed, right up until it closed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Hamdija Trnovac lost his job because the agency was closed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how did Hamdija Trnovac lose his job then? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when, the date, but it was probably at the end of May or perhaps the beginning of June. At the end of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know when the agency was closed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about then, because I went to see him at his home when he stopped working, in fact, and he told me what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, after Hamdija Trnovac lost his job, the agency was no longer working; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it wasn't. I'm not quite sure, but I think it wasn't working. I passed by the agency, and really there was no one inside, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Hamdija Trnovac's loss of job and the closing of the agency happened more or less at the same time, did it not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of an explosion at the Ferhadija mosque.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this explosion take place inside the mosque or in front of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to see the damage, and you saw that the damage was insignificant; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that the mosque was damaged as a result of that explosion? Did you see any damage at all?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that it is the mosque and not the building next to it that was damaged?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that it was the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the damage for us.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the walls of the mosque are made of stone. And on the street that leads from that crossroads to the Mejdan neighbourhood, as it was called in those days, next to an optician's, owned by Mr. Cengic, about 5 or 6 metres to the left, an explosive was thrown over the fence. It probably fell next to the mosque. And then the fragments damaged the stone wall of the mosque itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many mosques there were in Banja Luka in 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were at least 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1992, while you were still in Banja Luka, were there any that were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Re-examination, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now, what's going to happen, Mr. Fazlagic, is that Ms. Sutherland is going to ask you very few questions in addition to what she's asked you already. And then we'll see whether there are any questions from us, and short of that, that will be the end of it and you can go home. Ms. Sutherland, you may proceed. Thank you. Re-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, during cross-examination yesterday, Defence counsel Mr. Ackerman asked you some questions in relation to the alleged dismissal of Serbs from Atlas Prima Tours. He put to you the following scenario. This is on page 4340 of LiveNote. "I bet there is room, in your mind, for the possibility that what happened here was incorrect information was given to Mr. Kasagic in December by one of your former employees who said you had dismissed all Serbs and the only people left were two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs. That was then picked up by journalists and put in Glas, that you had dismissed all of the Serbs and that there were only two Muslims, two Croats, and two Yugoslavs left, and that Mr. Brdjanin heard about that from Glas, believed it to be true, and repeated it when he was interviewed. Now, that's a scenario that's probably true, isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to the article by the two journalists published in Glas in January 1992, did you give an interview which was also published in Glas?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to witness to be shown Prosecution Exhibit 5, which has been premarked as P536.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic, was an open letter also signed by the employees of Atlas Prima Tours published in Glas shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at that document you have in front of you, P536.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the headline of that article?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "False accusations."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the letter you referred to in your testimony yesterday, signed by the employees of Atlas?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically saying that the accusations that had been made in the article by the two journalists was incorrect.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P165, please. I'm sorry. Just before that's taken from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the date of the newspaper Glas, Prosecution Exhibit 536? Does it have a date on the top left-hand corner? A month?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month is January.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could just look at P165.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Court yesterday that the date of the actual article which mentioned Mr. Brdjanin was dated the 28th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, no, the day after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. The article you're referring to is entitled -- and excuse my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse my pronunciation, "Samo Kadrovi Lojalni Srpskoj BiH"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very good. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's dated the 29th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the open letter that was written by the Atlas Prima Tours employees published in Glas in January 1992 and the date of the article citing Mr. Brdjanin in April 1992, did Mr. Brdjanin or the Crisis Staff contact you to ascertain what in fact was the correct position in relation to the people that had been made redundant or had left Atlas Prima Tours?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. That document can be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday during cross-examination, Mr. Ackerman showed you P165, the ARK Crisis Staff conclusion terminating Atlas Prima Tours, dated the 3rd of June, 1992. Mr. Ackerman asked you the following question - and this is at page 4348 of LiveNote - "Again, Atlas continued to function and ignored that decision." Your answer: "No, we didn't ignore it, but in a kind of agreement, if I can call it that, we continued working for a while." Sir, after the 3rd of June 1992, decision was a directing body or board appointed in relation to the agency?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a director who was appointed, Mrs. Nada Crljenica, and she took over the responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned very briefly yesterday in your testimony, at page 4315, two people were appointed -- I'm sorry. "A board of management of Krajina Turist, two people were appointed to that board. I remember the name of only one, Mr. Dusko Lajisic." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What purpose was this board established for? For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was established so that immediately after Atlas was disbanded, then the work would continue under a new name in the same premises, which was still owned, which was still property of Atlas. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was their purpose to see through the termination of Atlas Prima Tours?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time that the board was established, after the 3rd of June, 1992 decision, Atlas Prima Tours continued to work while the board was doing whatever they were doing.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I don't know. Probably. They were preparing. They were carrying out preparations later when I had already left Atlas, I saw and found out that it had a new name. But up until that period, the crossover period, the name was still Atlas Prima Tours. The name, as a formality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Ackerman during cross-examination yesterday at page 4349, made the following comment after discussing the ARK Crisis Staff conclusion of the 9th of May -- and the decision of the 3rd of June, 1992. And Mr. Ackerman said: "It's probably true that it did exist, because nobody was paying any attention to the decisions of this supposed ARK Crisis Staff or implementing them in any way." Do you recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree with that? He didn't -- I'm sorry. Mr. Ackerman didn't give you an opportunity to respond to that comment. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 533. Your Honour, I have a highlighted version of Prosecution Exhibit 533 with certain of the text highlighted which I wish to show to the witness. Could he be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You can show the witness my copy, which is not highlighted. I would rather prefer that. Yours is not highlighted either, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. What I wanted to do was to actually show him the highlighted text, this document with the text highlighted and draw his attention to this highlighted text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see. I'm sorry. I misunderstood you. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Usher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at the highlighted portions of that document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Ms. Sutherland, on the ELMO we have exactly what we have in front of us, so we don't know which part you have highlighted for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Here is the English translation of those highlighted portions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just read the highlighted portions of that document.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Based on a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Banja Luka, decision number 03-531/92, dated 22nd of June 1992. I hereby issue -- and then the text follows. And then: "In accordance with the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka, number 03-531/92."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your view, did people pay attention and implement the orders of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we received officially just the decision on the cessation of the work of the agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlagic --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry. I have just one other issue that was raised in the cross-examination of Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, Madam Fauveau during her cross-examination asked the following question. And this is at page 4360 of the LiveNote. "Yesterday you spoke about General Talic and you said that you thought that his brother went to school with you. Do you remember that?"

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was her question. You replied: "Yes. I said that. But I said I wasn't certain whether that was General Talic's brother's brother or his brother." And then your answer continued. In order for us to be clear, who were you referring to when you answered Madam Fauveau's question?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The acquaintances of a colleague of Dr. Talic. We thought that that was so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The transcript reads: "I wasn't certain whether that was General Talic's brother's brother or his brother."

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM FAZLAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't you forget it, Ms. Sutherland? It's not going to change anything in the case, in any case, whether the witness -- the schoolmate was General Talic's brother or not, it's not going to change anything. And this fine distinction between a brother's brother and one's brother, frankly, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to leave it, Your Honour. I just wanted the transcript to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. But I don't think you're going to have it cleared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you keep getting a "da," "da," "da," and that's it. So Mr. Fazlagic, that's the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you for having come here to give evidence and for your cooperation with the -- with the Chamber, with the Prosecution, and also with the Defence teams. I thank you once more. You will now be escorted out by the usher and taken care of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I formally seek to tender the exhibits which were introduced through this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll go through them just by number. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened? What's wrong? Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. There was some communication going on between my co-counsel and my client. I have no idea what it was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Sutherland. Be patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's just a matter of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if everything is okay, I don't need to know, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's just what I was getting ready to tell you. Everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I only need to know if there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So you want to tender as exhibits documents P532 through 536; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Both numbers included.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. They are so admitted as exhibits in that order. And now we need to go -- the next witness is -- we have image distortion and the use of a pseudonym. Please Madam Fauveau, Mr. Ackerman, and Ms. Sutherland, do remember that. And I think we have to put up the screen before the witness comes in. First we have to pull down everything. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We shall remain in here? I think so, yes. We have seen it before, so we'll just make sure that it's done the usual way, the normal way. Where is the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He cannot bring in the witness before the curtains are drawn. Yes, there is, just behind ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just confirm the protective measures granted for the witness. Only facial distortion and pseudonym. No voice distortion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No voice distortion. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] This was decided yesterday. [Microphone not activated] Ms. Sutherland, do you expect to finish with this document today or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Finish with this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And the next one you reckon will take longer?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Three days, we think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Three days for the Prosecution, or that's including the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We're assuming that he will be finished completing his testimony within three days. That's including the cross-examination. But we don't know how much cross-examination either Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau would have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to be given a document on which there is a solemn declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth to this Tribunal in the course of your testimony. I would now like to invite you to take that document in your hand and make -- read out that statement loud. It's a solemn declaration that you are kindly asked to make before you start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Let me explain to you a few things before you start giving evidence. First of all, I would like to confirm to you that following your specific request, this Trial Chamber has granted you certain protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To hide your identity in particular. In other words, we have decided that no one, that is, members of the public, cannot see your face but they will only see a distortion of the image of yourself. And if you have the monitor in front of you, you will be able yourself to see, if you press "video monitor" you will be able to see how you yourself will be visible to the general public on video. And secondly, you are not going to be referred to by your own name. You have been given a nom de plum, a pseudonym. You are going to be referred to with a number, and that's also to protect your identity from -- hide your identity from the general public. Now, as you may have figured out, the three of us up here form this Trial Chamber, the Bench. I am the Presiding Judge, and to my right is Judge Janu, to my left is Judge Taya. And my name is Agius and I come from Malta. We will be hearing and determining and deciding this case. To your right is the team for the Prosecution. And the lady -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the third lady from you is the lawyer who will be conducting the examination-in-chief, who will be firing questions at you today. She is the counsel for the Prosecution in charge of you as a witness for the Prosecution. To your left in the front row you see four persons. Now, the first three, starting from the gentleman with the moustache and the beard, that's the Defence team for Radoslav Brdjanin, the three of them, the first three persons. The last person, the lady at the extreme right of the front row is Madam Fauveau, and she is the counsel for General Talic. The two teams are also entitled by law to ask you questions once the Prosecution has finished with its questions. Now, your duty here is a very simple one. You have decided -- volunteered to come forward and give evidence to tell us the truth, and therefore your duty is to answer the questions that are put to you. My invitation to you, in order not to have problems, is that you try to understand the question, each question, and then to answer that question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. That's the most important thing. If you try to answer more or if you try to answer "yes" or if you try to answer in a way in which you are not required to answer, then obviously it will take longer and we will have problems. So my invitation, again, please be precise, answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. And with that, I invite Ms. Sutherland to start her examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be shown this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, this is a piece of paper with your name on it. Don't read it. Just look at it and tell us whether that is your name or not. Just say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, can you show it, please, to the Defence teams. I -- Ms. Sutherland -- but I saw BT22? Yes. But that's going to be Exhibit P ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's going to be P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P537. BT22 is the pseudonym assigned to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's going to be 537.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 537, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it can be marked P539, because we've premarked two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have no problems with that. So this is being filed and it's being admitted as Exhibit P539 and it's been tendered and admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request if we can go into private session for a very short time so that I can ask some background questions of this witness which would reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? So we'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you provide a statement to members of the Office of the Prosecutor in October last year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That statement was read back to you by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were spoken to on Sunday, were you asked to review the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked if there was anything incorrect in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You advised, upon reviewing your statement, you wished to correct two things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the witness could be given a copy of his statement in his own language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can take you to page 7 of that statement, where the green tab is. In the English version, it starts on the last two lines of page 6.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the version you have in front of you, it starts the second full paragraph, the fourth line from the end of the paragraph. The sentence begins: "Samardzija then asked me about my other vehicles. I explained that only the Mercedes was in my name and the other vehicles were in my son's or other men's names." What did you wish to correct in this last sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Shall I make the correction straight away?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: All the vehicles were in my name, but they were used by my son, by my brother, and the workers in my company. And I only used the Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Still on page 7, where the blue tab is, the last sentence. And in the English version, this is halfway through the second full paragraph on page 7. The sentence begins: "The Serbs asked if they could come into my house because they wanted to search it." What did you want to correct about that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I just wish to say that they didn't ask. They just entered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could return that document to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were a member of the Communist Party from 1969 until 1986.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join another party, a political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: During the pre-election campaign, I joined the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you join the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I am -- I listened and followed all the programmes of the parties that were running in the elections. My opinion is that the SDA party in those days offered the best programme. Furthermore, I felt that parties like the SDS, with the emphasis on the Serbian Democratic Party, that that was a party I could not belong to, or the Croatian Democratic Union, I couldn't belong to that one either. They all had the adjective "democratic," at least in those days. But the programme of the SDA party was the most appealing to me, and that is why I became its member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any political rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any SDS rallies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was during the election campaign. There were public rallies in front of the Boska, next to the Boska in the cultural centre, in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any speakers at that SDS rally that you attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I can. Nikola Koljevic, Biljana Plavsic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Mr. Brdjanin, and many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically what any of the speakers said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: If you mean during the election rallies, all of them were saying that everything would be fine in Bosnia. They made big promises, and they appealed for unity --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: -- of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: If we're talking about the SDS rallies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend any SDS rallies after the multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: After the elections, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This SDS rally that you said you attended, do you recall the general theme of the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The gist of it was by an open appeal to the people that all the Serbs should give their voice for the SDS party, give their vote for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that was said at this rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I must admit that all the speeches were nationalistically intoned and that already then one could discern a call for Serbs and Serbdom, an appeal being made for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you some questions about the period after the mobilisation in 1991. Did you have meetings with the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the mayor of Banja Luka, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Mr. Predrag Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: We reported on the problems we were encountering. He took note of them, promising to take certain steps to eliminate those problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the time period these weekly meetings occurred in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The end of the summer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you reported on the problems that you were encountering. Can you tell the Court what sort of problems these were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was a difficult period in Banja Luka. People were mostly losing their jobs or had already lost them. There was the problem of shooting and violence by armed men that could not be explained. Then there was a problem of all possible kinds of mobilisations that they carried out. And we had to say what the difficulties were that we were encountering in the parts of town in which we lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these meetings held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The first meeting was held in the premises of the local community. The second meeting -- all the other meetings were held in the building of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attended these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: At the first meeting, there were representatives of the civilian, the military, and police authorities. So representatives of the civilian authorities, the military, and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meetings that you had with Mr. Radic in the municipal assembly building, who attended those meetings with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Do you wish the names of the people? Do you want me to give you the names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What positions did these people hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: People went to those meetings -- that someone believed to be influential among the population in those parts of town. So there were people of various backgrounds and occupation, ranging from manual workers to engineers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did these meetings last in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: For two, two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any meetings held in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: No. I apologise. That's a mistake. The meetings were in 1992, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When did the meetings with Mr. Radic begin, the meetings that lasted for two to three months? When did they begin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago I asked you about meetings that were -- that occurred just after the mobilisation in 1991. You spoke briefly about one meeting held in the local commune. And then you said that there were further meetings with Mr. Radic held in the municipal assembly building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you reported on incidents and problems that were occurring. Just so that I'm -- just so that it's clear, when did these meetings occur with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: At the end -- I may have made a mistake, but this is quite certain. At the end of the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you see any soldiers when they returned -- oh, I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Just going back to these meetings with Radic. When you discussed the problems that you were having and you reported several incidents that were occurring, what was Mr. Radic's response, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Mr. Radic promised every time that he would undertake all measures to avoid such incidents. However, every meeting was like a repeat of the previous one, and nothing was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ask you to do or not do certain things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. He told us in the form of advice and told us to tell others that we shouldn't be seen much in the streets, that we shouldn't gather in groups, to avoid contacts with the Serb soldiers, in order to reduce the risk and the possibility of conflict situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, can we stop for about two or three minutes, the time being until they change the tape, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you may go ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just before we had a short break to change the tape, you said that Mr. Radic told you that you shouldn't be seen much in the streets, that you shouldn't gather in groups, to avoid contacts with Serb soldiers, in order to reduce the risk and the possibility of conflict situations. Who are the "we" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He meant the Muslim population from the areas that we represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have any meetings with Mr. Radic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the question I began to ask you a moment ago: Did you see any soldiers when they returned from the front in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see them doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Well, at the time, Banja Luka was a town filled with shooting or even worse than that, if we can say that. It was a town full of armed people, lots of weapons, lots of upheavals, disorders. Everyone who was able-bodied, young, they were mobilised. It was a town of soldiers. Often they were drunk, and then they would fire on and on. In any case, this disturbed the normal population in Banja Luka and brought in a lot of discontent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they shooting at anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They fired everywhere, if one can say that. Most favoured targets were religious facilities, if they went through Muslim areas where there were mosques, then they would start shooting ceaselessly. Those mosques, all 16 of them, would later be destroyed. They fired at houses. They fired at shops. These were savage acts of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn to another topic. Do you know the accused Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first hear of Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I heard about him before the SDS party was formed. And when he arrived in Banja Luka, I learned some details about him, where he comes from, who he is, and what he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I think that was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what period of time that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He appeared on television often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: At first he was a deputy, I believe, in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was in the Assembly of the Serbian people. He was a Serb delegate, a Serb deputy. So he was often seen on TV and heard on the radio and appeared in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please ask the witness to place this within a time frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was my next question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because that was also included in your previous question, but he didn't answer it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what time frame did you see Mr. Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the period that you saw Mr. Brdjanin on -- how many -- sorry. How many times did you see Mr. Brdjanin on television in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I cannot give you the precise date. On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the programmes that you saw him on in 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He was often a guest on TV, and he would then make speeches. And some of the kind of speeches that he gave would absolutely terrify all non-Serbs in Bosnia and even elsewhere. These were mostly political speeches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what sort of speeches these were. What was the content of the speeches?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that we have a time frame for this particular question. And I'd ask that it be restricted to that time period which is relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman is right, Ms. Sutherland. Please regulate your question or rephrase it. You can even be very specific and direct the witness in this regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in 1992 can you please tell the Court the nature of the speeches that you heard Mr. Brdjanin give on television at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I said beginning, that these were political speeches. And they were intoned in such a way that the Serbs were being called to unite, to fight the aggressor, to triumph in combat operations, and there were also matters in everyday life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything specific that you remember Mr. Brdjanin saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: From his discussions, people cannot forget some terrifying, humiliating remarks. Almost unbelievable. He said, for instance, that Muslims were not a people, that they were nothing. He used to sometimes call us "Turks" or "those who became Turks." He would speak of a town. At that time, they were already calling it a state. They were talking about only 2 or 3 per cent of Muslims. It was terrifying. And then that he would then let the Muslims do the hardest types of work and how can anyone speak -- that this was a man who was saying that he would destroy all those in mixed marriages and their children. How could I accept this when I, in my own family, I have Serbs and we have children from mixed marriages. Such things cannot be forgotten. They're even hard to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear -- sorry. Did you see anyone else on television, giving similar sorts of speeches to Mr. Brdjanin -- to that of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: In 1991, 1992 almost all those who spoke on television they gave such speeches that they're hard to imagine by anyone who is normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention to the time period 1992. Do you recall the names of anyone else you heard -- you saw on the television, making similar speeches to that of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I was greatly surprised by Professor Gugo Lazarevic, which even today I find hard to comprehend that he used to be a professor of mine. And there are others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Most frequently, they were representatives of the military and the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you name them? This was your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among others, Mr. Radic, Mr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Vukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Mr. Vukic was at first the representative of the SDS party. Otherwise, he's a gynaecologist in Banja Luka. Then there was Mr. Milanovic. He's also a doctor from Banja Luka. And many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, if anything, what Dr. Vukic said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: One thing that remained with me, when he said through laughter, as a joke, that he would not charge for an abortion on any -- from any -- on any Muslim woman so that there would be fewer and fewer Muslims. This left a deep impression on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Radoslav Brdjanin on the radio in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many times you heard him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Not many times, but I did hear him. I did listen to him, because I believe he was a favourite of Nikola Deretic, who came, as far as I know, from Prijedor, and he was a speaker on radio, a newscaster, and he became a journalist. And I believe that he was pushing Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of what Mr. Brdjanin said on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin often spoke about the situation on the front. He spoke of some borders and establishing new states, about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina and such like. The strangest thing was when he was determining the borders, and he kept talking about Greater Serbia. So I was always amazed if it was possible that an intellectual could speak of such things or imagine such things. Had he ever heard of history? That left a deep impression on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall reading anything in newspapers which Mr. Brdjanin had said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During -- I'm sorry. During 1992 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what do you recall reading?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: In 1992, yes. For instance, how he was able to be ironic when he was asked, "Could now the Muslims who have remained, who are loyal citizens, could these Muslims have managing posts?" And he said, "No." See, these Muslims are now reading Politika, they're reading a Serbian newspaper. And his ironic answer was, "Yes, because it is the best newspaper." These are the kind of conversations that were held by Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now ask you some questions in relation to SOS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does "SOS" stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Serb defence forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw SOS in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: For the first time, I saw SOS members in the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They had military uniforms on, and they had red berets on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms. I saw them for the first time in front of the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal encounter with the SOS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They came to see me, and they transformed, so to speak, into blackmailers. They came to see me in the summer. And they asked -- they wanted to be my protection force -- protection force that I would have to pay for. They did this with many others, many other owners of shops and businesses in Banja Luka who were non-Serbs. From me, to start with, they asked for 1.000 Deutschmarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take them up on their offer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: No. I thanked them, and I said that I was satisfied with the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall seeing a red van in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time you saw this red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I think that was in 1992. But before it, there were others who had the same task as the red van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you think it was in 1992. Can you be more specific in relation to the month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was -- I'm certain that it was in the spring. I'm certain about the red van in the spring.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the persons involved with this van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Do you want names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are able, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Those were policemen, were members who were in the army centre in Banja Luka. And among them, as far as I knew and also according to the experiences of other people, there was Bosko Vuksan. With them also was Riza. That's what his nickname was. I don't know his real name. He was from Karanovac. And then there was Zuco. They addressed each other by nickname, so we did not know their real names. I know that Zuco came from the Rudarska Street, that he was a small businessman, and that he made tombstones. And they often switched in their groups, and I know one whose last name was Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I think we have to stop here for the time being. We have a break. We will resume at quarter to 5.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just before we broke, you mentioned several names who -- of people who were involved with this red van. What did you see these people doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The red van, like the other vans in Banja Luka, represented the greatest evil, especially this red van which was synonymous with fear for the non-Serbs. They went literally from house to house. They carried out searches. They arrested people in the streets. They beat people until they were unconscious. They would take them into custody into the former army centre. Others to the Mali Logor. They would round people up in the street or from their homes. Usually, in addition to weapons, they carried wooden baseball bats with which they beat people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they dressed? I'm sorry. How were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They were dressed in blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they rounded up people in the street or from their homes. Can you name anybody --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that you saw being picked up by this red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: An unlimited number, if necessary. Do you want the names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Ismet Rakovic, Angijad Gunic, Fahret Redzepovic, Reuf Gunic, (redacted), Jasmin Hrnic. Do you want some more?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the people you've just named, which of these people did you personally see being picked up by the red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I intentionally listed all the people that I saw. As for those I heard about and whom I saw after the beating, as I said, the list would be endless. If you wish me to give you the names, I'll do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just deal with the people that you've mentioned to begin with. Were these people picked up individually or in a group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It depended on the time and the place. If they were looking for them in the houses, then they would take them one by one. If they caught them by surprise in the street, then they would arrest several at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just describe for the Court what happened when you saw these people being picked up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They would throw them into the car while beating them. And this is Jasmin, [redacted], and they opened the door of the van and started beating them so fiercely that people were screaming with pain to produce a better effect and for them to achieve their goal, which in my opinion was intimidation and expulsion of the non-Serb population.
