They would open the back door of the van so that these screams and cries could be heard outside for people to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the condition of these people after they had left the red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: All the people who came out of the red van were visibly, visibly beaten up, with swellings and bruises. They could move with difficulty. They could hardly move at all after a certain amount of time. They would urinate blood, most of these people who were beaten up. It was horrible. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these people tell you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: As these were [redacted], and it is customary and normal for such people to be visited, quite a number of them were not very well off. So I felt it my duty to take them some fruit juice, coffee, or something to eat. And anyway, I would have visited them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was this occurring, people being picked up by the red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They would come to our neighbourhood almost every day. Sometimes several times during the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people also being picked up in this red van from the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: When they were at the market, for instance, which is in the centre of town, then they would carry out so-called raids, which would be quick searches of Muslims, or rather, non-Serbs, because they treated the Croats and all others in the same way, to see whether they had the appropriate documents allowing them movement in town. If they didn't have those permissions for movement, then those people would be rounded up and taken away. And this also happened very frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that you also heard about others who were picked up by this red van. Can you name them, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I can. As I know the people [redacted], I will go in this order. Fahret Redzepovic, Angijad Gunic, Armin Gunic, Dzevad Sistek, Ibrahim Gunic, Hanzalija Gunic, Bernard [phoen] Gunic, Samir Asic, Rokic -- Samir Trokic. I apologise. Asic is Asmir, Asmir is the first name. And Samir Trokic. Reuf Gunic, [redacted], Mukic -- Sead Omukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of these people that you either saw or heard being picked up in the van, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted]. And all those who were arrested and beaten up were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, were people also taken to coffee bars in this red van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. If I can put it that way, they organised orgies, one could say. This gave them pleasure. Our pain gave them pleasure. And I remember an example, when in Gornji Seher, in a coffee bar called Cobanin, or "shepherd," they brought in young men they had picked up in Novoselija, and they demanded that Jasmin Hrnic climb up on a table. They gave him a beer bottle instead of a microphone for him to use and sing Serbian songs. And then a few moments later, they would push him off the table and step all over him. They were simply taking their pleasure in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who owned this coffee bar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The owner -- earlier on, this was a shop, and then it was changed to a coffee bar and the owner was a Serb, a few kilometres away from Seher. I think he comes from the village of Bukvalek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal experiences with this van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court your experience.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the autumn of 1992 -- no, the winter. There was snow on the ground. When in my yard, seven of them arrived, led by Bosko Vuksan. They entered the house, and that they just said that they wanted to look for something. Among them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Ms. Sutherland, but -- sorry about that, Ms. Sutherland, but it was important. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were explaining to the Court your experience with the red van. And you said that seven persons had arrived, led by Bosko Vuksan, and they had entered your house. Can you continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. A person that they addressed as Komandir, he was sitting down and the others were standing. He assigned two of them to search the ground floor level and that two of them go with my wife to examine the shop. He said to them to pay attention to letters, literature, books, weapons and to look closely into the bedrooms to see what was being read at night, which they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ordered to do anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They said that they had come to carry out an examination and also on the basis of a document that they had found in the house of Bajazit Jahic. And on this document, there was a list of members of the Party of Democratic Action. And he ordered me to go with them to show them these addresses. I think that this part of our contact was a provocation. What they wanted was (redacted) to see me in the red van, to see me as an associate of theirs, as a collaborator who was assisting the Serbs in carrying out something ugly. They showed me a list, and I had to go with them to point out the houses, one by one. When my wife asked them -- asked Vuksan not to take me away, he said, "Don't be afraid. He'll be back." And indeed, I had to do what I considered to be a nasty piece of business. I had to take them from one house to the next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you pointed out certain houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They would leave me in the van with the door open so that everyone could see me. They started from Izmet Gunic. They wanted his house first. And then Hazira Gunic's. Then they were looking for Samir Barucija, Buzdalek Sefket, and the younger Gazic, Sead's son. I don't know the young man's name. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you pointed out these houses, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They would leave me, as I said, in the van with the door open, and they would enter, with those bats, into the houses. I don't dare say anything. They didn't bring the men out, but according to what I heard after when I was released to go home, the same story was repeated. They would break the glass, the paintings on the walls, and couple this with threats: "Why aren't you going away? Why aren't you moving out? What are you waiting for?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, did you ever go to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you attend the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I received a summons to report to SUP. Nothing was stated on this document as to the reason why, but in those, days there were checkpoints. We called them checkpoints. There were -- they were places with Serb police there and some sort of guards. At first, they wore the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army and, later on, camouflage uniforms. They had different uniforms. No one could come or leave --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. When you got to the SUP, were you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you interviewed about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Two police inspectors -- at least, that is how they addressed them -- took me in to Mr. Drago Samardzija's office, a man I knew from before. And they asked me where my vehicles were and why I hadn't delivered them earlier on and why I hadn't responded to an earlier call. And I explained that I couldn't pass through the checkpoints. So simply, he asked and demanded where my vehicles were, which were needed by Republika Srpska for their army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you tell him is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I told him, literally, what we have just corrected in my statement, and that is that I only have the Mercedes -- that I only had the Mercedes which I had handed over to the police when they came to my house and drove it off, and I took out of my pocket, as I'm doing now, a certificate which I received certifying that my vehicle had been confiscated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that receipt dated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: If you wish to look at it, I haven't -- I didn't see the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher. [Microphone not activated] Let us see it first.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Let's see it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you show it to Ms. Sutherland, please, and then afterwards to both Defence teams, please. Ms. Sutherland, do you have a copy -- does the Prosecution have a copy of that receipt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you to -- pardon? Yes. But first I would like to know whether the Prosecution wants a copy of that receipt to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the Defence will use this document, so could we have copies of it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have copies made of that document. But it is not being tendered as an exhibit as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I look at it -- I'm sorry. May I look at it one more time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I realise that it won't be tendered, but we may do it during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The position is as follows: The document will be handed back to the witness. Obviously the witness has made it available to the Chamber and to the parties. And that entitles the Chamber to have copies made of that document, which obviously we can make use of in the course of the cross-examination. That applies to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prosecution as well, both at this stage and as well in the re-examination case. Sir, may I ask you to -- in case we don't finish with your testimony today, may I ask you to bring that document with you tomorrow, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the month that your Mercedes was confiscated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't recall. I don't know. There is no date on the document, but I know it was summer. It was warm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your signature appears on that document, does it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who the other signature belongs to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Before I tell you, I have to tell you that the -- when the vehicle was taken, the people who came to get it, as far as I know they were working on the security in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just pause there, sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: And they were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you questions about that in a moment, but I asked you: Can you tell the Court who the other signature is on that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: On this place of the signature, that was the director of Blik, who was the director of the company -- a clothes company, a retail -- they were making uniforms for the army, for the Serbian army. He was a new person. I don't know him from before. He had a large beard. And he was short and dark. He did not introduce himself. But because of the protocol, he had to sign it, because I asked for the certificate that my vehicle was confiscated, and he then placed his signature there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe for the Court how your vehicle was confiscated and the persons involved in that confiscation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They came between 2.00 and 4.00 p.m. I'm not quite certain when. It was sometime in the afternoon. And they said that they needed the vehicle for the new director of Blik --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: -- who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to keep interrupting you. You said "they came between 2.00 and 4.00 p.m.." Do you recall the names of the people who attended at your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Of course. Before that, I met this policeman whose name was Crnobrnja. And he was accompanied by a short policeman. He was more working like a car mechanic, or better to the point he knew about cars. And his nickname was Srbo. And Crnobrnja told him that he should prepare the vehicle and to start the engine. And the third person was the director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this Crnobrnja -- I'm sorry for my pronunciation -- do you know where he worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Crnobrnja worked as a member of the unit that was located in the factory of a leather produce. And the director was Sulejman Deumic. They made leather and fur items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the first name of this person called Crnobrnja -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I don't know exactly his first name, but his last name is definitely Crnobrnja. He used to be a waiter, and he was a newcomer to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were questioned in the police station about your car, and you told them that it had -- your Mercedes had already been confiscated, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Mr. Samardzija said that he knew about the Mercedes, but he also said that I had a Peugeot car, a luxury car, and I also had three Volkswagen vans and that it was my duty to hand them over as soon as possible for the needs of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that you told these people that these vehicles were being used by other persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their reaction to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Samardzija, unfortunately, shouted at me. And he said, "You're lying. You have all the vehicles." I tried to explain to him that the Peugeot car was driven by my elder brother and that one of the Volkswagen vans --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Witness. Don't mention the name of the other people, because that will -- may reveal your identity. If the Court or Defence want you to name that person, then we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Thank you. So what I said was that one vehicle had been sold, that the second vehicle had been destroyed by the machine-gun bursts of Serb soldiers, and the third one was not in working order. But he did not believe me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: And already then they started to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They started to beat me, first on my face and then later all over my body. It was a terrible feeling of helplessness. I was put on a round stool in the middle of this room, and these two people whom they called inspectors, they were standing each on my sides, they flanked me, and any answer of mine that didn't suit them, they would beat me. And the hardest ones to bear was in the -- in the knees and in that area here. And if one of them knocked me to the ground, then the other one would lift me up, and then the other one would do the same for his colleague. It was absolutely horrific. I asked Samardzija to give me protection. I thought he knew me. But no help came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: For a long time. For a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What injuries did you suffer as a result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: My teeth were broken, and here I think you can still see the traces of strangulation. I would feel it in my mouth. I would feel the teeth that were broken in my mouth. It was horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is pointing to his throat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person called Jovan Sovilj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, did you know what his occupation was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: According to him, he was a deputy commander for security in the town. And he was based in Deumici [phoen], in his factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who his commander was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: His commander was Mr. Stevandic. I think his first name was Dusan. Certainly it was Stevandic. He was blond. He was a large man.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 537. This is the document provided in B/C/S with two pages of translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of General Talic objects to these documents because they do not bear any dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Before I respond to Madam Fauveau, if this document can be marked Prosecution Exhibit P538. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not 537?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No. There's been another exhibit premarked 537. In response to Madam Fauveau, this document is undated; however, the Prosecution intend having a witness date this document somewhere between June and October 1992. This document comes -- was seized from the Banja Luka Corps, and it was disclosed to the Defence on the 2nd of August, 2000. The Prosecution intends obtaining a full translation of this document, but at this stage we only have the front cover and page 7 translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is admitting the document, both in the B/C/S version and in the English version, because the fact that it is undated does not automatically exclude its admissibility in evidence, subject, of course, to further proof which may result in establishing the date for this document, and with the understanding, if there is the need for it -- Mr. Ackerman, and Madam Fauveau, this is on the face of it a list of individual members of the group of Light Infantry Brigades. And all it shows is the name and the rank. Is it important for you to -- and the office. Is it important for you to have it completely translated in its entirety, or -- because I understand that there are words which are recurring, for example, pukovnik, and Komandant, and Nacelnik staba [phoen]. If those are translated, that should be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really not in a position to do much more than shrug my shoulders at this point because I don't know what it is, I don't know what the Prosecution intends to do with it, I don't know what the Prosecution intends that it stands for or anything. Obviously, I have not been able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Leave it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Chances are I don't have any objection, but I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, Ms. Sutherland, you will consult further with the Defence teams. Should a proper, complete translation of this document be required, then go ahead with it, as you are required to do by the Rules. Otherwise, if there is an indication of the meaning in English and in French of the various porucnik, kapetan, pukovnik, so that we understand what we are looking for -- are looking at, then it should be enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We do intend having the entire document translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Translated. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the B/C/S version could be put on -- sorry, the English translation could be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the title of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: "Overview of individual members of the group of the 4th Banja Luka Light Infantry Brigade."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it continue? I'm sorry. Can you read the front page, the cover page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The front page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The front page of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: "Military secret. Strictly confidential. Overview of individual members of the -- of the command of the Light Infantry Brigade -- Light Infantry Brigades, brigade commands, battalion commanders, company commanders, and of independent platoons," with the code 01302583. And then there is the initials K.K.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you just turn to page 7 of that document. Sir, the ERN number on that document is 01302589.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you don't have the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the title of that page, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. "Military secret. Strictly confidential. Overview of individual members of the 4th Banja Luka Light Infantry Brigade command."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the name at number -- next to the number 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Number 1, Dusan Stevandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He's a major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He's a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the name next to number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Jovan Sovilj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: This should be sergeant, first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Intelligence and security commander. Intelligence and security commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also read the name at number 22.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes. Number 22, that's the person, Milorad Crnobrnja, sergeant. He was a commander of the platoon command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This last name that you just read, is that last name the same as the -- one of the people that came with you when your -- that came the day your car was confiscated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified earlier that when they came to confiscate your car, they said that it was for the use of the military.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say which unit in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: They said that this was needed for the director of the company that was making military equipment for the Serb army, and he was personally present at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If that document can be returned to the registry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to ask you some questions in relation to a murder that you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992. Do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you aware of -- how do you recall the exact date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I spoke to the wife of the killed Avdo Softic, and she established the date for me, which was the 5th of December, 1992, and I stand by that date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this murder occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The murder occurred in the immediate vicinity of the house of the murdered, Avdo Softic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone else killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: This happened in the street -- Avdo Gazic Street or Gozic Street. And the person who was killed was Ramiz Zdenac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what happened on that day in relation to that incident.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Because of the situation that we found ourselves in, we were forced to walk along a side road which we called Stari Put, "old road", and this is where we hid from the main road, so that we wouldn't have any contact with the Serb army. And in order to avoid any unpleasant situations. That night, it was a complete surprise for all of us who found ourselves on that road. There was an armed Serb soldier who passed on that road. It was the first time that one of them used that street. He didn't say hello to us. He didn't greet us, although we knew him. But we were all surprised. We were surprised that he was there. After a few moments, shooting was heard. First there was a short burst and then a long burst. There was panic, and I thought that if the shooting continued, that this was directed at me, because I had been informed before -- several Serbs had told me that I was on the list for elimination. So I lay down alongside a fence. And after a short while, I heard somebody asking for help. Avdo Softic was shouting for help but not to help himself but Ramiz to be helped, and he said about himself, "I am finished." We ran to Ramiz. And at that time when I came round, the shooting had stopped and I saw the murderer, who was walking away in haste from the site. And the late Ramiz started to slide down the fence. Avdo was on the ground on the other side, perhaps a few metres away from him. It was obvious -- it was visible with Ramiz that he could not be helped. There was blood in the chest area. And the only thing that we could hear was the gurgling of a man who was dying. There was terrible panic among us, all of us who were standing nearby. We ran towards them to help them. It was that kind of situation when the words fail you. It is hard to describe. And somebody suggested that we should call -- that was -- that person was Omer Saranic. He had a small Fiat vehicle. And he was asked to take Avdo Softic to the hospital. When we put him in the car, it was obvious that he was finished. In the stomach area and the lower part of his body was all covered in blood, but he was still conscious. He knew and he was able to speak. But when Omer speeded up to the hospital, he died on the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you knew the perpetrator. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The man's name was Zeljko Ceko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He lived --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: He lived in the immediate vicinity of our neighbourhood, maybe a kilometre away. Some people called the area Brda and others Novoselija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were Avdo and Ramiz wearing, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Ordinary civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: No. I think that in 1992, and later too, a Muslim with weapons would be tantamount to suicide. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Avdo or Ramiz doing anything to provoke the soldier before he fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I already said that we had passed on to our people instructions as to how they should behave, that they shouldn't provoke anyone, that they shouldn't engage in any disputes or any contacts. And especially in this case, these were two exceptionally quiet, good, and honest men, so that any provocation is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you notice what sort of weapon Ceko was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Ceko had, in my view, a long rifle, a rifle -- it may have been a light machine-gun. I think it was a rifle or a submachine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, do you know whether any -- whether there have been any proceedings in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I inquired everywhere as to what had been done against this criminal; however, all I know is that he was taken in for questioning as he was on leave, allegedly that his punishment was that he had to go to the front, which we, in those days, found unbelievable because he was already at the front. So that I believe to this day and I claim that I saw him after that crime, passing by. He was not sentenced. If going to the front line is punishment, according to them, he had already been punished and not for this particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to turn to another topic and ask you some questions about life in Banja Luka during 1992 for non-Serbs. Can you describe for the Court the atmosphere in Banja Luka at this time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I can only do my best. But to really describe the situation of hunger, fear, killings, shooting, and everything else that is not deign of a civilised man, that is what Banja Luka was like. People were left jobless earlier on. All the people who refused to respond to the call-up for mobilisation and who refused to take part in the Serb army were automatically dismissed. People were left jobless, and they needed to feed their families, their children. And as time went by, the situation became worse and worse. People were left without homes. All it took was a Serb fighter to point a finger at an apartment that he wanted for that apartment to become his. Fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you travel freely outside Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: No one could move around freely - I think I said that at the beginning when I mentioned those checkpoints - who did not have the appropriate permit. These were issued at first by local communes and then later by the military department, which meant that all those who were fit to serve either had to go to the front lines or to leave Banja Luka. There was no freedom of movement. Who refused to go to the front line, he actually sentenced himself to detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did your -- when did family members -- your family members leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: My daughter left in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did she leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: At the time, there were stories about terrible crimes being committed by those Serb troops; among other things, rape. I had --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did she leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I was afraid of this rape that was being mentioned all over the place, because my daughter was beautiful and young. Unfortunately, her youth was taken away from her and her work and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how did your daughter come to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: In Banja Luka -- I can't call them enterprises or firms or what they were that were formed in Banja Luka for the resettlement of non-Serbs from Banja Luka. These were organisations that had their own buses or rented those buses, I don't know exactly, but one such organisation existed in Mejdan, across the River Vrbas, as we would put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the Mejdan settlement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: The Mejdan settlement, or neighbourhood, where there was an organisation for the transport of non-Serbs. This organisation was headed by a lady called Perka. I don't know what her surname was. Her name was Perka. And daily there would be up to a thousand people there, waiting in line and applying and begging to be taken out. Then there was an organisation with the Red Cross, another one in Budzak. And later, I heard there were others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your son and wife left in April 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you leave with your -- with your son and wife at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I will have to admit I was sorry -- of everything I had as a result of very hard work, and I was sorry to leave it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: Through the mediation of international organisation, the UNHCR, I was taken out on the 15th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was my assessment that it was high time. And after all the beatings, persecution, and the worst was in September 1993 when among the Serbs, there was some kind of a rebellion in the Serb army and we the people of Banja Luka felt the effects very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: It was an operation that was known as --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just finish that sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: "Black September."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken in the red van to the JNA Dom and severely beaten whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I was taken in a police car to the old JNA Dom, or club. And if you believe me -- and I can swear to that -- from the top of my head to my big toe, I was black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month was this in 1993, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I already said, September, because the operation was called "Black September."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you one question about the red van. Was it common knowledge that what this -- what was happening in relation to this van? Was it common knowledge in Banja Luka what was happening to the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I dare to say today the worst evil of Banja Luka for the non-Serb population was the red van. They destroyed so many young lives, expelled so many people that the red van will go down in history -- in the history of our people. And I believe that we should recount the story to young -- our young generations. It is a horror. It is impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I just ask one more question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop for a couple of minutes to have the tape changed, because otherwise whatever you ask will not be recorded anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, you may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the red kombi, was it common knowledge in 1992 what was happening to the non-Serbs with this van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: All the people of Banja Luka, the non-Serbs knew what evil the red van stood for. I've already said once. People fled. One's blood froze. There was so much fear and panic that it is hard to describe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have decided that I now wish to tender the receipt. If that could be marked as Prosecution Exhibit number P540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, there is obviously not going to be any major problems with that, except that I think we have to acknowledge the witness's right to retain the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I would suggest is that he lets us -- lets us have that receipt of the Mercedes again; we have it photocopied now, and various copies of it real size and a couple of copies we magnify it a bit, just in case that's needed. And we return the original to him, because I don't know what the position is, but he may require it maybe in civil proceedings in his country. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever -- did you ever retain your Mercedes-Benz -- regain possession of your Mercedes-Benz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT22
utterances.text: I did not, and I believe I will never see it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I would ask just to go into private session for a short time to ask a few questions in relation to his property and financial situation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? Yes. We'll go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. So I understand, Ms. Sutherland, that you would like, having concluded with your direct examination of the witness, that you would like to tender documents as exhibits -- some documents related -- relating to --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. Just before you move on to that, if Exhibits 539 and 540 could be tendered under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And these would be ...? May I have a look at them, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 539 is the witness's name and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's taken for granted. We always admit that under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 540 is the receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the receipt, Madam Registrar, in its original size, is 540.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These documents, Your Honour, are from a military court file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the exhibit number would be 538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go with the disclosure number, one by one, because I think -- is it just one disclosure number or several?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was going to -- I'm sorry. Ms. Gustin has just informed me it should be 537, the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of this bundle of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 538 is the Light Brigade document. I intended to give you the date of the document and then give it a specific number. For example, 537.1, 537.2, 537.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then the English would be the A, and the B/C/S would be the B. Before I do that, Your Honour, these documents relate to the Defence Exhibit tendered by Madam Fauveau, DT7 on the 11th of April, and it gives the Court a complete picture of this incident. So the first document is a record of interview with the accused compiled on the 10th of December, 1992. That's a two-page document. That is 537.1. The next document is dated the 10th of December, 1992 with a number 106/92. It's the cover sheet -- it's a letter enclosing the record of the on-site investigation carried out on the 5th of December, 1992, regarding the murder of Avdo Softic and Ramiz Zdenac. If that can be marked 537.2. The next document, Your Honour, is also dated the 10th of December and has the same number, 106/92. And it's a ruling from the investigating judge. It's a one-page document. If that can be marked 537.3. It's a ruling that the suspect Ceko be remanded in custody for one month. The next document is dated the 12th of December, 1992. It's addressed to the investigating judge Banja Luka military court, request for an investigation to be carried out. It's a two-page document. If that could be marked 537.4. When I'm saying how many pages --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: .4. When I'm saying the number of pages, Your Honour, I'm referring to the English translations. The next document is dated the 8th of January, 1993. And it's a ruling by the president of the chamber of the Banja Luka military court. It's a ruling to extend the custody for two months of the accused Ceko. It's a two-page document. If that can be marked 537.5. It's also got a number, KV 1/93. The next document is dated the 12th of January, 1993. It's from the military prosecutor, addressed to the military court in Banja Luka, consenting for the release from detention of the accused Ceko as he is immediately going to a war unit. If that document could be marked 537.6. Your Honour, with this document, we are requesting a revised translation because in the top right-hand corner, it says "Military Prosecutor's Office at the Command of the/?2nd//?Krajina/Corps." One can see though, if you compare that document, which is signed by the military prosecutor Spasoje Pisarevic. If that document is looked in conjunction with document 537.4, signed by the same person, it is clear from the English translation on the front of that document that it's the 1st Krajina Corps command, not the 2nd Krajina Corps. We are going to try and provide the Translation Unit with a better copy of the document. And if they cannot work out that it's the 1st Krajina Corps, to put the word "illegible," as opposed to 2nd Krajina Corps. The next document, Your Honour, is dated the 12th of January, 1993. Reference number 336/92. And it's a ruling signed by the investigating judge Stupar, releasing Ceko from custody -- immediately releasing him from custody and sending him to his war unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm lost. Can you please give me the draft translation number, the number -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this would be ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The next document is dated some seven years later, on the 18th of February, 2000. It has a reference number at the top KIK-151/93. It's a record of hearing. It's a one-page document. I'm sorry, Your Honour. The next document is out of order. I think if we can perhaps put these in order -- in chronological order. I'm sorry. So the document dated the 12th of January, 1993 is marked 537.7. The next document in chronological order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about the chronological order, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. So we've marked 537.8. The next document is dated the 8th of May, 1993, and it's an indictment against the accused Ceko. If that can be marked 537.9. The next document, Your Honour, is undated, but it's a ruling stating that the hearing shall be postponed sine die and ex officio defence counsel shall be appointed. The ERN number -- the translation ERN is 03046252. If that can be marked 537.10. The next document, Your Honour, is dated the 10th of April, 2000, reference number, IK number 151/93. It's a ruling on assignment of counsel. If that can be marked 537.11. The next document is dated the 10th of April, 2000. Reference number also 151/93 MT. If that can be marked 537.12. That's an acknowledgement of receipt from Defence counsel. The next document is dated the 23rd of April, 2001, number K-160/00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just been informed that the document I marked as 537.8, which was a record of hearing, and the page that I just told you a moment ago was undated, which we've marked 537.10, is in fact page 2 of 537.8. So 537.10 then now becomes the ruling on assignment of counsel dated the 10th of April, 2000, reference number 151/93. The acknowledgement of receipt by the Defence counsel, also dated the 10th of April, 2000, which was marked 537.12, is now 537.11. The next document is dated the 23rd of April, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, I'm going to stop you. I think I am going to send you -- better return to you all these documents. Please take them home with you and come back tomorrow afternoon first thing with the proper -- because I am getting confused now. I mean, I had them all here, and now I have to take what was numbered 10 and put it behind number -- .8, and 12 becomes 11, and 11 becomes -- and I think -- I think we need to do this. And we will have them admitted tomorrow afternoon. I think it's easier that way, because otherwise there's going to be a confusion. And even I was seeing a lot of resistance on the part of the registrar. So I think we'll have to stop here. I thank you, sir. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one thing, Your Honour. Do you want -- I will put the documents in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the so last two pages of transcript will not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry, Ms. Sutherland. Do it whichever way you like, provided we don't -- we won't have any room for confusion. Sir, you will need to come again tomorrow. You will be cross-examined by the Defence teams tomorrow. In the meantime, you will be taken care of and escorted out of this room. But before that, we will leave ourselves so that they will drop the curtains so that no one can see you going out. Thank you. And good evening, everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
